claims.text: An integrated high-throughput CALPHAD, molecular-dynamics, and in-situ experimental workflow can determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, melting volume change, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the HEA family.
The integrated workflow will provide high accuracy and efficiency.
The target initial state is a near-equiatomic, single-phase solid-solution HEA at room temperature.
CALPHAD calculations incorporating configurational entropy and mixing enthalpy can predict fusion properties.
Atomistic MD simulations can capture elevated-temperature atomic diffusion and local structural evolution in HEAs.
Combining in-situ STEM observations with MD simulations can characterize HEA thermal behavior and melting-related structural changes.
Refractory HEAs typically require a measurement range of approximately 2000–2500 K to span the solid-to-liquid transition.
Local atomic ordering and clustering evolve during melting.
Evolving local ordering and clustering mediate the balance between configurational entropy and mixing enthalpy in the liquid.
Thermodynamic modeling can estimate or rationalize phase stability in HEAs.
Matching computational results to real-time experimental data refines fusion-property predictions.
The high configurational entropy characteristic of HEAs governs their melting behavior.
Predicted melting temperatures, fusion enthalpies, fusion entropies, and melting volume changes will agree with experiments within approximately ±10% across diverse HEA compositions.
Single calorimetric methods or isolated CALPHAD or MD models are less efficient and less broadly applicable than the integrated workflow.
Rapid phase decomposition or non-equilibrium transitions during melting can limit the applicability of the equilibrium workflow.
Accuracy depends on thermodynamic databases and interatomic potentials being properly calibrated for multicomponent alloys.
Standard equilibrium CALPHAD and MD may fail to capture rapid transient non-equilibrium melting phenomena.
DSC and aberration-corrected STEM can directly provide the complete validation set of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and melting volume change.
Errors exceeding ±10% or failure to reproduce experimental composition trends would falsify the proposed workflow.
